summary: For ages 9–11: identify the main ways humans harm the ocean (plastic pollution, overfishing, oil spills, and acidification from CO2), and grasp the counter-intuitive key fact that roughly 80% of marine pollution originates on land — carried by runoff, litter, sewage and farm chemicals down rivers and drains to the sea — not mainly from ships. Learners name each harm and how it affects a specific marine animal, trace the invisible inland→river→sea pathway, and follow a harm as it cascades through the food web. Builds on prior ecosystem/food-web systems thinking.
misconceptions: 'Most ocean pollution comes from ships/dumping at sea' — the core misconception; ~80% is land-based via runoff.
'Pollution only affects the spot where it enters' — not seeing it spread and cascade through the web (e.g. via currents, bioaccumulation).
'Overfishing just means fewer of one fish' — missing the knock-on collapse of the wider ecosystem.
'Plastic goes away / breaks down quickly' — not knowing it persists and fragments into microplastics eaten by animals.
'If I live far from the sea, my actions don't affect the ocean' — ignoring the inland-runoff pathway.

activities.title: Live a day on land, then watch it reach the sea
steps: Look at a scene split between an inland town-and-farm on top and the ocean below.
Perform ordinary land actions: spread fertiliser on a field, drop a bottle by the kerb, flush the drains.
Trigger the rain and watch each pollutant wash into a stream, down a river, and out to sea.
Observe the consequences: the fertiliser feeds an algal bloom, and the bottle drifts out to sea and slowly breaks into fragments that a seabird or fish swallows, mistaking them for food.
Overfish a fish stock and watch the loss ripple visibly through a food-web overlay to other species.
Read a running source tally that shows land vs ship contributions, with land arriving at roughly four-fifths of the total.
activities.insight: Most ocean POLLUTION (about four-fifths) starts on LAND, often far from any ship, and travels via drains, runoff and rivers to the sea. Ocean harms, including pollution and overfishing (which happens at sea from fishing boats), can then cascade through the marine food web rather than staying at one spot.

activities.title: Harm–animal cards: naming harms through their victims
steps: Match each harm to a specific animal and effect: plastic bag → turtle that eats it mistaking it for a jellyfish; plastic fragments → seabird with a stomach full of plastic; oil spill → otter with coated fur; overfishing → fewer fish left for seals and seabirds that eat them, disrupting the food web; CO2 → more acidic water that makes it harder for shellfish and coral to build and keep their shells and skeletons.
Name at least three distinct ways humans harm the ocean.
For one harm, state out loud or in writing exactly how it hurts a named animal.
activities.insight: Each ocean harm has a concrete, nameable effect on real animals; plastic persists and fragments into microplastics, and CO2 is an invisible gas that still pollutes the water.

activities.title: One bottle, many victims: tracing a cascade
steps: Trace a plastic bottle dropped on a city street hundreds of miles from the coast to the sea, naming the route (drain → river → sea).
Follow a toxin or microplastic from plankton up through fish to predators, noting that one input can reach many animals that never touched the plastic directly.
Explain whether banning all ships would mostly stop ocean pollution, and why or why not.
Explain how carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, can count as ocean pollution.
activities.insight: Pollution does not stay where it enters: it spreads through currents and bioaccumulation up the food web, and because the bulk comes from land, stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched.

activities.title: Talking it through with a marine biologist or a sea turtle
steps: Ask a marine-biologist character 'how does MY town's rubbish reach the sea?' and respond to their follow-up questions about the runoff pathway.
Discuss why overfishing hurts more than just one fish, explaining the web disruption in your own words.
Hear a turtle character recount mistaking a plastic bag for a jellyfish, and discuss what could be done differently.
activities.insight: Ocean harm has a values and agency dimension — who is responsible, whether distant inland behaviour matters, and what we can do — alongside the factual mechanism.

activities.title: Check: pollution sources, main cause, and a traced cascade
steps: Name three ways humans harm the ocean.
Answer where most ocean pollution comes from — land or ships — and give the approximate share.
Work a scenario that traces a specific land activity through runoff to a cascading effect in the ocean food web.
activities.insight: Learners can demonstrate naming harms, identifying the land-based majority source, and tracing a land activity to a cascading marine effect.

checkQuestion: A child says 'the ocean gets polluted mostly by ships and oil spills out at sea — so if we stopped ships leaking, the ocean would be basically clean'. Do you agree that ships are the main source? Where does most ocean pollution actually come from, and how does it get there?
checkAnswer: No — most ocean pollution comes from LAND, not from ships. Around 80% of it starts on land: plastic litter, farm and sewage run-off, and chemicals wash down rivers and drains and out to sea, plus carbon dioxide from burning fuels dissolves into the water and makes it more acidic. Dramatic oil spills are real but are a small share of the total. So stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched, because the bulk pours off the land.
